OpenStax 8.1: implicit memories are not part of consciousness and cannot be consciously recalled but are demonstrated in performance; procedural memory stores skills such as riding a bike.

problem: H.M. did not keep all his memories from before the operation. He had a partial retrograde amnesia, first reported as covering about the 3 years before surgery and later argued by Corkin to reach back about 11 years; his older memories, such as from school years, were preserved. 'Kept memories from before the operation' reads as complete sparing.
proposed: In 1953, at age 27, H.M. had surgery on both sides of his brain to control severe seizures; afterward he forgot daily events almost as fast as they happened, though he kept most older memories from before the operation. (Card 033.c2: change 'yet he kept memories from before the operation.' to 'yet he kept most of his older memories from before the operation.')
evidence: Squire 2009: surgery in 1953 at age 27, bilateral medial temporal lobe resection; he forgot daily events nearly as fast as they occurred; he had a partial retrograde amnesia for the 3 years before surgery (later estimated at 11 years), with early memories seemingly normal.
MIT News (Corkin): profound amnesia existed with an above-average IQ; immediate memory, like remembering a telephone number, was intact.
MIT News: H.M. (whose full name, Henry Gustav Molaison, was disclosed only after his death) died a year ago (2008) at 82; Squire 2009 refers to him only as H.M.
Squire 2009: Milner's mirror-drawing task; H.M. acquired the skill over trials and showed excellent retention across 3 days, yet had no recollection of having done the task before.
Squire 2009: H.M. is probably the best known single patient in the history of neuroscience; he continued to be studied for five decades until he died on December 2, 2008.

MIT News (Corkin): the hippocampus and neighboring cortex are critical for long-term declarative memory; motor skill learning was preserved, relying on networks outside the medial temporal lobe; memory is compartmentalized.
MIT News (Corkin): asked how he felt about the tests, he replied, "What they find out about me helps them to help other people."

Noba: the encoding specificity principle (Tulving and Thomson, 1973): to the extent a retrieval cue (the song) matches the memory trace of an experience (the party), it will be effective in evoking the memory.

Murre 2021 (Royal Society Open Science) on Godden and Baddeley 1975: divers learned auditorily presented word lists on land or underwater and recalled them in the same or other context; the original found better recall in the matching context.
Murre 2021: environmental context-dependent memory measured with free recall is now well established, although in many circumstances the effect is rather weak (d around 0.25).
Murre 2021: virtually all textbooks I have used describe the classic study on environmental context-dependent memory by Godden and Baddeley.
Murre 2021 abstract: sixteen divers studied word lists on land or underwater (a heated indoor pool in Amsterdam); contrary to the original, recall in the same context was not better.
Murre 2021: the original used open water near Oban, Scotland, in cold conditions; more replications are necessary to establish whether the classic study deserves its privileged position.
Murre and Dros 2015: a single-subject design; Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve is based on seven months of experimenting, often up to three sessions per day.
OpenStax 8.3: in 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself, producing his famous forgetting curve; Noba cites Ebbinghaus 1885/1913.
Murre and Dros 2015: the Don Juan fragments he tried were too variable in meaning, so he introduced nonsense syllables with more uniform characteristics; Noba gives dax, bap and rif as examples.
OpenStax 8.3: your memory for new information decays quickly and then eventually levels out (the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve).
Murre and Dros 2015 (University of Amsterdam), abstract: one subject spent 70 hours learning lists and relearning them; the results are similar to Ebbinghaus' original data.
Murre and Dros 2015: rows were studied until recalled correctly twice in succession; intervals 20 minutes to 31 days; 25 repetitions then 20 on relearning is a 20% saving.
Murre and Dros 2015: memory traces that cannot be recalled or recognized can still show savings; savings is still used as a sensitive method.

Bergman and Roediger 1999: The War of the Ghosts was unusual for the English college students who seem to have been Bartlett's subjects; Bartlett tested 15 min after study and again weeks, months, or even years later.
Roediger and DeSoto: the story is disjointed, contains supernatural elements, and is rather difficult to understand.
Roediger and DeSoto: if encoding or perceiving is a construction, recalling the event later requires reconstruction; schemas can lead to recalling a beach umbrella that was not present.

Bergman and Roediger 1999: Bartlett's observations had never been successfully replicated, partial attempts were unsuccessful; they replicated them, and after 6 months most of what people recalled of the story was distorted in some form.

Roediger and DeSoto: errors increased over repeated retellings; the stories got shorter and changed systematically as subjects introduced errors rationalizing bizarre elements, sometimes 'remembering' elements to explain them; remembering is guided by schemas.
Bergman and Roediger 1999: an example of normalization would be replacing 'canoe' and 'hunting seals' with 'boat' and 'fishing.'

Roediger and Karpicke 2006 abstract (via Europe PMC): students studied prose passages and took recall tests or restudied; after 5 min restudying was better, but on tests 2 days or 1 week later prior testing produced substantially greater retention, even though restudying increased confidence.
Noba: the act of retrieval itself makes the retrieved memory much more likely to be retrieved again, a phenomenon called the testing effect or the retrieval practice effect.

Dunlosky et al. 2013 abstract (via Europe PMC): most students report rereading and highlighting, yet these techniques do not consistently boost performance (low utility), so other techniques should be used (e.g., practice testing instead of rereading).
OpenStax 8.4: distributed practice: study across time in short durations rather than cramming; memory consolidation takes time, and studying across time allows memories to consolidate.

Vlach and Sandhofer 2012 (Child Development): see Ebbinghaus 1885 for the first study on the spacing effect; 'The spacing effect is arguably the most replicable and robust finding from experimental psychology.'

Dunlosky et al. 2013 abstract: of 10 techniques, practice testing and distributed practice received high utility assessments because they benefit learners of different ages and abilities across many criterion tasks.

Roediger and DeSoto: Bartlett argued that remembering is guided by schemas, general organizing structures that aid encoding and guide retrieval, but can lead to errors such as recalling a beach umbrella that was not in the scene.

OpenStax 8.3: Loftus and Palmer (1974) asked how fast cars were going when they (smashed, collided, bumped, hit, contacted) each other; 'smashed' raised speed estimates, and a week later that group was more than twice as likely to report seeing broken glass, though none was shown.
Noba (Laney and Loftus): misinformation after an event contaminates memories; hundreds of studies; from small details of a perpetrator's appearance to objects as large as a barn that wasn't there.
Noba: subjects were more likely to say yes to 'Did you see the broken headlight?' than 'Did you see a broken headlight?' (Loftus, 1975).

Noba: a researcher-introduced story of being lost in a shopping mall; after being asked on three occasions, a quarter of subjects came to believe they had been lost in the mall (Loftus and Pickrell, 1995); Murphy et al. 2023: 25% in the original.
Murphy et al. 2023 abstract (via Europe PMC): preregistered direct replication, N = 123; 35% coded as reporting a false memory of getting lost in a mall, compared with 25% in the original.
Noba: once false memories are implanted, whether through complex methods or simple ones, it is extremely difficult to tell them apart from true memories.

OpenStax 8.3: in 1984 in North Carolina, Jennifer Thompson identified Ronald Cotton from photos and a lineup; her testimony helped convict him; after 11 years in prison DNA evidence showed he was innocent.

OpenStax 8.3: she said 'I think this is the guy', the detective reinforced her choice, and by the trial she had absolutely no doubt; Wells and Quinlivan (2009) blame suggestive procedures such as confirming the witness's choice.

Steblay, Wells and Douglass 2014: the feedback effect was originally demonstrated by Wells and Bradfield (1998) with the Target store security video and a culprit-absent lineup; 'Good, you identified the suspect' inflates retrospective certainty.
Steblay et al. 2014 abstract: meta-analysis involving 7,000 participants; confirming feedback robustly inflates retrospective judgments of certainty, view and attention.
Steblay et al. 2014: the gold standard is a double-blind procedure in which the person conducting the lineup is not aware which member is the suspect, preventing feedback cues.
Noba: a fair lineup is one in which the suspect and each foil are equally likely to be chosen by someone who read the eyewitness description but did not witness the crime.
Steblay et al. 2014 abstract: testimony-relevant witness judgments should be collected and documented, preferably on video, before feedback can occur.

Wixted and Wells 2017 abstract (via Europe PMC): under pristine conditions (fair lineups, no administrator influence, immediate confidence statement) high-confidence IDs are remarkably accurate; initial low-confidence IDs are error prone.
OpenStax 8.1: memory is the set of processes used to encode, store, and retrieve information; encoding is input, storage is retention, retrieval gets information back into awareness.
OpenStax 8.3: Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams (1979) found most Americans don't know which drawing is the real penny; we only encode enough to distinguish it from other coins.
Noba: if you fail to encode information you will not remember it; it has been well documented that distraction during learning impairs later memory (Craik et al., 1996).
OpenStax 8.2: memory is not like a video recording; even flashbulb memories are frail; parts are stored in different places and put back together when remembered.
OpenStax 10.1: motivation describes the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal.
OpenStax 10.1: homeostasis is the tendency to maintain a balance, or optimal level, within a biological system.
OpenStax 10.1: deviations from homeostasis create needs and drive states that direct behavior; low blood sugar induces hunger, and eating returns blood sugar to normal.
OpenStax 10.1: once we have engaged in a behavior that successfully reduces a drive, we are more likely to engage in it whenever faced with that drive in the future.
EBSCO Research Starters: incentive is said to 'pull' and drive to 'push' toward a goal; incentive motivation is a determinant from without, drive from within; both jointly determine behavior.

EBSCO: bar-pressing for water in a Skinner box normally requires water deprivation, but under special conditions the animal will press the bar to drink even without being water-deprived (nonhomeostatic drinking).
Maslow 1943, A Theory of Human Motivation, Psychological Review 50: physiological, safety, love, esteem and self-actualization needs.

problem: 'Must be satisfied before' states the strict ordering that the tree rules say not to teach and that Maslow himself qualified in the same 1943 paper ('not nearly as rigid'; people are partly satisfied in all needs at once). The card line 'Lower needs come first' is fine in context of 042.c3; the fact text overstates.
proposed: In Maslow's theory, lower-level needs generally take priority over higher ones: someone struggling to find enough food is unlikely to focus on how others see them.
evidence: Maslow 1943: the hierarchy 'is not nearly as rigid as we may have implied'; most members of society are 'partially satisfied in all their basic needs and partially unsatisfied in all their basic needs at the same time.' OpenStax 10.1 gives the strict textbook reading.
Maslow 1943, p. 382: 'the desire to become more and more what one is, to become everything that one is capable of becoming.'
Maslow 1943, p. 386: 'it is not nearly as rigid as we may have implied'; p. 388: people are partially satisfied and partially unsatisfied in all basic needs at the same time.

Scientific American interview with Bridgman, Cummings and Ballard (2019 paper): the pyramid was traced to consulting psychologist Charles McDermid's 1960 Business Horizons article; no trace of a pyramid in Maslow's writings.
Tay and Diener 2011 abstract (via Europe PMC): across 123 countries, associations of well-being with fulfillment of specific needs were largely independent of whether other needs were fulfilled.
OpenStax 10.1: intrinsically motivated behaviors are performed for the personal satisfaction they bring; extrinsically motivated behaviors are performed to receive something from others.

Lepper, Greene and Nisbett 1973: children at the Bing Nursery School on the Stanford campus, selected for initial interest in drawing with magic markers; the extrinsic reward was a 'Good Player Award'.
Lepper et al. 1973, Table 1: mean free-choice time drawing was 8.59% (expected award), 16.73% (no award), 18.09% (unexpected award), observed 1-2 weeks after the sessions.
OpenStax 10.1: the overjustification effect: intrinsic motivation is diminished when extrinsic motivation is given, which can create a dependence on extrinsic rewards for continued performance.
Deci, Koestner and Ryan 1999 abstract (via Europe PMC): meta-analysis of 128 studies; all tangible and all expected rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation; positive feedback enhanced it.

OpenStax 10.1: tangible rewards (money) tend to have more negative effects on intrinsic motivation than praise; if the reward is a surprise rather than expected, intrinsic motivation tends to persist (Deci et al., 1999).

Baumeister et al. 1998: hungry participants who skipped a meal ate radishes while faced with chocolates and freshly baked cookies; a few picked up cookies to sniff them, but no participant bit into the wrong food.
Baumeister et al. 1998, Table: time on unsolvable puzzles, radish 8.35 min, chocolate 18.90, no-food control 20.86.

Baumeister et al. 1998: choice, active response, self-regulation and other volition may all draw on a common inner resource; Hagger et al. 2016: self-control as a limited resource that becomes depleted, a state known as ego depletion.

Hagger et al. 2016 abstract (via Europe PMC): although a meta-analysis found a medium-sized effect, subsequent meta-analyses questioned the size and existence of the effect and identified instances of possible bias.
Hagger et al. 2016 abstract: k = 23 laboratories, total N = 2,141, standardized protocol; d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15] encompassing zero.
Vohs et al. 2021 (Psychological Science): preregistered multilab project, k = 36, N = 3,531; preregistered analyses did not find evidence for a depletion effect.
